#3364. Jaren Johnston Is Releasing a Solo Album. What Does That Mean for the Cadillac Three?

When the Cadillac Three walked offstage at the Born and Raised Festival in Pryor, Oklahoma, on Sept. 13, 2024, fans of the Southern rock band didn’t realize they’d just witnessed the trio’s last public performance. A week later, the Nashville band announced they were canceling the remainder of the year’s gigs so that singer-guitarist Jaren Johnston could prioritize his health. The group has yet to return to the road.

Johnston, a songwriter behind radio hits like Tim McGraw’s “Meanwhile Back at Mama’s” and Keith Urban’s “You Gonna Fly,” had been through the wringer. His father, the musician Jerry Ray Johnston, died at 65 in 2022, and the Cadillac Three’s busy touring schedule didn’t allow the frontman time to heal. The future of the group, known for hard-hitting songs like “Tennessee Mojo” and “White Lightning,” was in doubt. Drummer Neil Mason pivoted to songwriting and artist management; lap-steel player/bassist Kelby Ray played guitar in the house band for Taylor Sheridan’s country-music series The Road.

This Friday, Johnston will resurface with his debut solo album, The Guest Room, a collection of 13 songs written and recorded in the spare room of his home.

So, where does that leave the Cadillac Three? Johnston tells Rolling Stone’s Nashville Now podcast the band members are slowly starting to pick up the pieces.

“The three of us just want the best for the three of us, each one of us. When I had to come off the road, they understood,” he says. “Obviously [they were] not happy about not being able to play shows and not being able to explain to everybody why. But they probably saw it coming, a little bit.”

Johnston says he, Mason, and Ray met at a local Mexican restaurant in Nashville recently to reconnect. “All we did was sit and laugh for an hour and a half,” he says. “You can’t mess that whole thing up.”

#3363. This Actively Exploited Chrome Vulnerability Is Putting Your Browser at Risk

If you've seen an uptick in security updates as of late, you're not alone. AI models have become very good at finding new security vulnerabilities throughout 2026. Researchers and hackers alike are increasingly relying on these models in their individual pursuits: Hackers want to find these flaws to exploit them, while researchers want to block hackers from doing so. Microsoft's latest Patch Tuesday update included more than 1,400 patches; meanwhile, Apple's latest security update fixed two iMessage flaws that let both bad actors and innocent parties alike access texts they shouldn't.

Whether you use a Mac or a PC, you probably browse the web with Chrome, or a Chromium-based browser. As it happens, Google's web browsing platform is the latest to receive an important security update—but it's far from the first important Chrome update of the year.

As reported by The Hacker News, Google released a new update for Chrome on Monday that patches nine security flaws. While all vulnerabilities are important to patch, one in particular is more serious than the rest: CVE-2026-125350, a use-after-free bug in Chrome's XML component.

Use-after-free vulnerabilities happen when the system frees up a memory location, but a program tries to access it anyway. It's a glitch in programming, but it offers bad actors an opportunity to break into your system. At worst, it allows arbitrary code execution, or, in other words, gives hackers the ability to run their own code in the app or system.

That's bad enough on the surface, but, unfortunately, Google confirmed that CVE-2026-125350 has an active exploit in the wild. The company is keeping other details close to the vest, but it's dangerous nonetheless. At least someone, somewhere, has used this flaw against a target, which puts all Chrome users (as well as users of Chromium-based browsers) at risk.

What's more, this isn't Chrome's first active exploit of the year—this is its eighth. The company is playing catch-up with hackers looking to target users of its browser, which makes sense, seeing as Chrome is by far the world's most popular browser.

If you're using Chrome on your computer, you'll want to update it as soon as possible. Make sure you're running at least versions 157.0.8103.50/.51 on Mac or PC, or 157.0.8103.50 on Linux. To check, click the three dots in the top-right corner of your Chrome window, then go to More > Help > About Google Chrome.

Other Chromium-based browsers may not have the update yet, but they are affected by this flaw. If you use browsers like Microsoft Edge, Opera, or Brave, keep an eye on your updates to install any of the latest patches.

#3362. Report: Apple saved over $5 billion in taxes through Singapore and Ireland in 2026

A new Financial Times report reveals how Apple saved billions in taxes in 2026 by shifting profits through Singapore and Ireland. Here are the details.

A few days ago, Apple published its annual Form 10-K, as required by the SEC, containing detailed information about its financial performance and operations for its 2026 fiscal year.

Included in the form, as the FT noted, is information regarding how Apple reduced its tax bill by billions of dollars through its operations in Singapore and Ireland.

For years, Apple’s tax arrangements in Ireland were the subject of scrutiny, culminating in a 2024 ruling by the EU’s top court that required the company to pay €13 billion in back taxes. Apple completed the payment in 2025.

That came a few years after Apple announced plans to bring most of its $252 billion in overseas cash back to the US, following tax reforms introduced during Donald Trump’s first administration.

Since then, to discourage companies from shifting profits to countries with lower tax rates, more than 130 countries have agreed to introduce a minimum corporate tax rate of 15% for large multinational companies, as part of a 2021 initiative coordinated by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD).

Under the agreement, companies that pay less than 15% in a particular country may face additional taxes to make up the difference. The new rules also resulted in an additional $2.5 billion in taxes for Apple in Singapore in 2026, according to the company’s SEC filing.

Ireland adopted the new rules in 2024, followed by Singapore in 2025.

Back to the FT’s report, it notes that new US accounting rules now require publicly traded companies to disclose when their taxes on overseas profits differ significantly from the 21% US federal corporate tax rate.

These new requirements revealed that Apple saved $2.7 billion in taxes through Singapore in 2026, surpassing the $2.6 billion it saved through Ireland.

If Apple had been taxed on all of its global profits in 2026 at the US federal rate, it would have incurred a total bill of $33bn — demonstrating the scale of the $5bn tax reduction it received from booking profits in Ireland and Singapore. The company incurred corporation taxes totalling $27bn this year.

The FT also noted that Apple’s effective tax rate in Singapore fluctuated around 10% between 2023 and 2025, but is expected to approach 15% under the new rules. Singapore’s standard corporate tax rate is 17%.

#3360. Summer Walker’s Label LVRN Fires Back With Breach of Contract Counterclaim

The independent label that signed Grammy-nominated R&B star Summer Walker early in her career is denying allegations that it locked her into an oppressive contract and misappropriated money, and it’s firing back with its own breach of contract claim against the singer.

In a new court filing obtained and first reported by Rolling Stone, Atlanta-based Love Renaissance Records, known as LVRN, strongly denies allegations of breach of contract and fraud made by Walker in her August lawsuit. “At no time has LVRN acted in bad faith, been stubbornly litigious, or caused Walker unnecessary trouble and expense,” the new 14-page filing submitted in Fulton County, Georgia, states.

The label and management firm then accuses Walker of being the one withholding funds. According to the filing, Walker failed to pay LVRN a 15 percent share of income from business opportunities it allegedly secured for her, as well as a 20 percent share of her songwriting performance royalties. The company also claims Walker stopped paying its agreed-upon 7 percent share of proceeds from her Finally Over It tour in 2026, after she initially made such payments.

“Walker has acted in bad faith and been stubbornly litigious, such that LVRN is entitled to recover its resulting attorneys’ fees,” the new filing states. It’s asking the court to dismiss Walker’s original complaint, rule in its favor on the breach of contract counterclaim, and award damages in an amount to be determined at trial.

In a statement to Rolling Stone, Walker’s lawyer, Keith Moten, said LVRN’s counterclaim “does nothing to change the fundamental issues at the heart of Summer’s lawsuit, nor does it diminish their obligation to account for their actions.”

“It is particularly disappointing that, rather than meaningfully addressing Summer’s serious allegations, LVRN is now seeking additional money from the very artist whose talent, hard work, and success helped build its business,” he said. “We strongly dispute LVRN’s counterclaims and remain confident in the legal and factual grounds supporting Summer’s lawsuit.  She remains steadfast in her pursuit of accountability, fairness, and the freedom to move forward with her career on her terms.” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

Walker’s manager, Aubrey Banks, tells Rolling Stone that the musician respects the legal process but will “continue to advocate” for herself and other artists while the case is pending. “Summer is a human being before she is an artist. Like anyone else who’s devoted over a decade to their work, she deserves fair treatment, transparency, and good-faith dealings. No one wants to work for 10 years with no career advancement, raise or promotion,” Banks says. “It’s just not fair. The music industry should not be exempt from the fundamental standards of fairness, dignity, and respect we expect in every other profession.”

In her lawsuit, Walker accused LVRN of improperly diverting money from her touring, recording, marketing, and merchandising budgets, and failing to pay her revenue generated by Amazon and YouTube webpages featuring her name and likeness. She claimed the company concealed financial information, betraying the trust she placed in the label as a 19-year-old artist.

“Summer is in a new phase of her life,” Moten said in a previous statement to Rolling Stone. “She’s been through a lot in her life, personally and professionally. She’s a mother now, and she doesn’t trust blindly anymore. She’s ready to fight for herself, her freedom, and her peace.”

Walker’s lawsuit alleges breach of fiduciary duty, breach of contract, and fraudulent concealment. She is asking the court to declare her 2017 agreement with LVRN “void and unenforceable.” She’s also seeking compensatory and punitive damages in amounts to be determined by the court. In August, Walker informed Interscope that she would soon stop working under the agreement. “This letter shall serve as official notice that, effective Aug. 27, 2026, Ms. Walker will no longer render service under the agreement by reason of the fact that the agreement is no longer enforceable,” her letter to the label said, according to court filings.

In its Oct. 9 complaint, Interscope claimed Walker’s “failure to deliver” all the recordings required under her contract would leave her liable for damages. #3353. Mississippi Is Sending a Democrat to the Senate

Of all the spectacular Democratic upsets in 2026 midterm elections — a statewide sweep in Texas, the first senator elected by the state of Kansas in almost a century, an underdog stunner in South Carolina — the most shocking victory of all came in Mississippi.

The race to represent the ruby red state of Mississippi in the U.S. Senate was called for Democrat Scott Colom on Wednesday, just over a week after the election. Colom, a district attorney, defeated Republican incumbent, Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.

Colom led Hyde-Smith by roughly 2,000 votes the day after the election, and steadily increased the margin before the Associated Press called the race Wednesday at 5:58 p.m. ET.

“I think that anybody who can look at the math should be able to know where this is going,” Colom told reporters on the morning after the election. “It’s going to: Scott Colom is the next United States senator. I’m confident in that.”

He was right, and the victory is especially sweet. In 2023, Colom, then a state prosecutor, was nominated by President Joe Biden to a lifetime appointment on the federal bench. That nomination was blocked by a single senator from his home state: Hyde-Smith.

Breaking with her Republican colleague, Sen. Roger Wicker, who backed Colom’s selection, Hyde-Smith cited Colom’s “opposition to legislation to protect female athletes” (a reference, apparently, to his decision to sign an open letter condemning the criminalization of gender-affirming care), as well as a single political donation he got four years prior from a PAC that had received funding from George Soros.

Three years ago, Colom wrote a letter asking Hyde-Smith to reconsider the decision; she refused. Had Hyde-Smith not spiked his nomination, Colom told The New York Times in May, “It is fair to say that I would not have resigned from the federal bench to run for Senate.”

Colom made Hyde-Smith’s tone-deaf response to the rising cost of living a centerpiece of his insurgent bid to replace her. One viral ad produced by the Colom campaign showcased Hyde-Smith’s comment, in answer to a question about the beef prices, that “You have so many proteins to choose from.” Rather than pick another protein, the spot urged voters to “Pick another senator instead.” It resonated, as Mississippians appear on Wednesday poised to do exactly that. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

Up until the point in late October when President Donald Trump flew to Mississippi to rally his supporters behind Hyde-Smith’s reelection effort, few political observers expected the race to be close. Only three polls were done of the match-up, compared to dozens of surveys conducted in higher-profile contests in Michigan and Texas. But in the waning days of the campaign, as it became clear Colom was mounting an unexpectedly strong challenge, former President Barack Obama and former Vice President Kamala Harris both traveled to Misssippi to boost Democratic support for his bid.

Colom’s win marks the first time a Democrat has represented Mississippi in the Senate since the prominent segregationist John C. Stennis retired in the 1980s.

Colom’s victory is even more remarkable considering the fact that Ty Pinkins — the Democratic candidate for Senate in 2024 — chose to run as an Independent in the general election this fall, siphoning off nearly 20,000 votes.

In spite of those challenges — and an emergency infusion of more than a million dollars from the GOP’s Senate Leadership Fund — Colom was victorious.  Trending Stories Sade Are Not Attending Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Induction Ceremony The ‘You Can See Everything’ Interview You’ve Been Waiting For Bob Dylan’s Meeting With Pope Leo: People Fixated on the Hood, But the Hands Spoke Volumes Megan Thee Stallion and Daniel Radcliffe Reunite for Season Two of ‘Reggie Dinkins’

Hyde-Smith herself may be more surprised than anyone by that fact: Speaking at an election night party on Tuesday, she was already celebrating, boasting to supporters, “I blocked Scott Colom from being a federal judge and you blocked him from being a U.S. senator.”

Asked on the next morning to respond to Hyde-Smith’s premature declaration, Colom called on a classic Southern expression: “Bless her heart,” he said.

#3351. Today’s macOS updates fix security gap involving eMudhra certificates

Apple today released macOS updates that address a security gap involving compromised eMudhra certificates, after initially blocking them in Safari, Mail, and other apps in October. Here are the details.

A few weeks ago, Mozilla reported that private keys of eight intermediate certificate authorities operated by eMudhra, an Indian digital certification company, had been compromised.

In essence, these certificates are used to establish trust in digital certificates that verify website identities and enable secure connections.

With access to the compromised private keys, bad actors could potentially create fraudulent certificates that appear legitimate, allowing them to impersonate websites and intercept sensitive user information.

In response to the compromise, Apple began automatically blocking the affected certificates on October 19, followed by additional protections on October 23.

These changes were delivered through automatic certificate configuration updates, meaning users didn’t need to install a macOS update to be protected.

While these measures protected Safari, Mail, and apps that use Apple’s networking and security frameworks, they didn’t cover all of macOS, as certain command-line tools, including curl and git, could still accept the compromised certificates.

At the time, Apple published a support article with instructions for administrators to manually address this remaining security gap, while promising a fix in a future macOS update.

Today, Apple updated the document to confirm that the fix is now available.

As Apple explains, macOS 27.2.1, macOS 26.7.3, and macOS 15.8.3, released earlier today, prevent the affected command-line tools from accepting the compromised certificates, eliminating the need for administrators to manually address the issue.

The updates also remove five root CA certificates from /etc/ssl/cert.pem, including three additional eMudhra certificates that weren’t part of Apple’s original manual workaround.

Still, for users who are unable to install the latest macOS updates, Apple continues to provide instructions for manually addressing the issue in its support document, along with the names and SHA-256 fingerprints of the 12 affected certificates and five root CA certificates removed by the updates.

Apple also notes that “some apps and tools include their own list of root CA certificates and don’t use Apple’s block or /etc/ssl/cert.pem,” and advises users to contact the developer of those apps and tools.

#3349. Apple Intelligence completes regulatory registration for iPad and Mac in China

Apple has completed an important regulatory step ahead of Apple Intelligence’s expected launch in China this December. Here are the details.

In late October, Apple published a press release on its Chinese Newsroom website confirming its intention to launch Apple Intelligence in China this December, as part of iOS 27.3.

Apple went on to release the first iOS 27.3 developer beta a few days later, allowing users in China to test Apple Intelligence ahead of its public launch.

In its press release, however, Apple also noted that the initial rollout would be limited to iPhones, as support for other platforms was still pending regulatory approval.

Now, as spotted by Reuters, Apple Intelligence “has been ‌registered for use on tablets and laptops in China, Shanghai’s cyberspace regulator said on Monday.”

For context, generative AI services must complete a regulatory registration process before they can launch publicly in China.

Apple Intelligence, which, in China, relies on Alibaba’s Qwen model to power certain AI features, had already received regulatory approval for iPhones in July, following months of delays and negotiations with Chinese authorities.

With today’s registration, Apple has cleared another regulatory hurdle ahead of Apple Intelligence’s launch in China. However, the company has yet to confirm whether iPad and Mac support will also arrive in December.

#3348. Elijah Wood Says “Muscle Memory” Kicked In Playing Frodo On ‘The Hunt For Gollum’ Set

Elijah Wood told Deadline tonight that playing Frodo again after more than two decades was “beautiful and surreal and it felt like no time had passed.”

Wood reprised the role earlier this year on director Andy Serkis’ new Middle-earth set tale, The Hunt For Gollum.

The actor has spoken in anticipation of returning to the part, but these may be his first public observations after having done so.

Serkis confirmed yesterday that principal photography for the film has now wrapped.

The Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum reunites beloved figures from across Middle-earth, including Ian McKellen as Gandalf, Wood as Frodo and Lee Pace as Thranduil. New actors announced for the film include Anya Taylor-Joy, Kate Winslet, Jamie Dornan and Leo Woodall. Serkis directs and returns as Gollum in the film. Watch on Deadline

“I think it really is a creative ‘getting the band back together.” Wood told Screen Rant before production in January. “It’s very much that core original group getting back together to tell this story that will feel like a really fun exploration of this character that we all love so much.”

Wood spoke tonight about being on set in his costume and hobbit feet again.

“It felt like stepping back into time. You know, looking down…having this sort of muscle memory that I’ve seen these feet this way. I know this wardrobe. And that feeling is so wild. It’s so transportive. Suddenly 27 years are gone and you’re back in it again.”

Elijah Wood on returning as Frodo for ‘The Lord of the Rings: The Hunt For Gollum’ pic.twitter.com/srVYx98Ud4

The Hunt for Gollum follows Aragorn’s perilous quest to capture Gollum before the creature can reveal the One Ring’s location to Sauron. The story, much of it developed from Tolkien’s footnotes, is set between the events of The Hobbit and The Fellowship of the Ring.

Last month, Serkis posted a video slideshow from the set. One of the final images shows what looks to be Wood as Frodo entering Bilbo’s hobbit house. You can watch it below.

Warner Bros. Pictures will release The Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum worldwide on December 17, 2027.

#3347. Arnold Schwarzenegger Calls for Democrats and Republicans to ‘Work Together’

Arnold Schwarzenegger stopped by Jimmy Kimmel Live to promote his new film, The Man With the Bag, and took the opportunity to reflect on being a Republican in today’s political climate.

Kimmel asked the movie star and politician if he is still a Republican early on in their conversation. “Yeah I’m a Republican, absolutely,” Schwarzenegger confirmed, explaining that a “traditional Republican is someone that admires the Republican party for having free the slaves.”

“This is the history,” he explained of the party. “This is what I’m about. Someone that has given those slaves American citizenship and has given them the right to vote is Republican.”

“This sounds like all of the opposite things the Republican party stands for now though, doesn’t it?” Kimmel responded.

“It doesn’t mean I have to change my philosophy,” Schwarzenegger said. “I have my philosophy. The Ronald Reagan philosophy, who created the air resources board in California so we can regulate our own air and reduce our greenhouse gases and pollution in California. That was done by Ronald Reagan, by a Republican. Nixon created the EPA. … So those are the kind of Republicans that used to go and work together with the Democrats and got things done. This is the kind of Republican that I am.”

“Unfortunately I think you’re the only one of them left,” Kimmel noted.

“No, I don’t think I’m the only one left,” Schwarzenegger acknowledged. “But this doesn’t mean that we should give up. The bottom line is we have just seen now what some people call the blue wave. I call it a tidal wave or a tsunami. It’s not really a wave anymore. But the bottom line of that is that now the Democrats go in there and they have the majority. And then the Republicans will go in there and they have the majority. And this is how it goes back and forth and back and forth.”

He added, “And it has been going back and forth like this for the last 20 years. And what happened in the last 20 years? None of them did true immigration reform. So we are still fighting over immigration. None of them participated in reducing our debt. None of them created a health care system where where everyone is insured.” Trending Stories Sade Are Not Attending Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Induction Ceremony The ‘You Can See Everything’ Interview You’ve Been Waiting For Bob Dylan’s Meeting With Pope Leo: People Fixated on the Hood, But the Hands Spoke Volumes Megan Thee Stallion and Daniel Radcliffe Reunite for Season Two of ‘Reggie Dinkins’

Schwarzenegger explained that if one party tries to do something by themselves it’s “bogus.” “What you have to do is the Democrats and the Republicans have to work together like we did when I was governor of California,” he said. “This is the only way you can accomplish something rather than always pointing fingers and accusing each other of things and calling each other names. No. You have to get together and accomplish and be a public servant rather than a party servant. There’s a difference.”

Elsewhere in the interview, Schwarzenegger reflected on Donald Trump asking for his support in 2016 when he initially ran for president. The former California governor explained that he felt he couldn’t endorse Trump’s campaign because they disagreed about certain issues, including climate change and pollution.
